summary: Summation No. 33 covers non-military Occupation activities in Japan for June 1948 (data mostly for April-May). Politically the month was dominated by the Nishio political-funds scandal, the Diet budget deadlock, and the Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee's probes of donations and hoarded military supplies, along with rifts in the Democratic Party. The 28 June Fukui earthquake devastated Fukui city and threatened textile rehabilitation. Economic sections report postwar peaks in coke, vacuum tubes, watches and silk fabric, a growing coal output, and new trade machinery: Boeki Cho's direct dealing authority, a $60 million raw-cotton credit and a sterling payment agreement. Labor reports union membership (6.55 million), left-right struggle and wage standards. Social sections cover new pharmaceutical and narcotics laws, repatriation, the Diet's rescinding of the Imperial Rescript on Education, and information programs. Historians will find detailed statistics, war crimes trial figures, land reform totals, and party and Diet legislative detail.
highlights: House of Representatives rejected nonconfidence in Deputy Prime Minister Nishio 209 to 178 over unreported political funds.
Earthquake of 28 June destroyed about 70 percent of Fukui city; 3,195 died there and 9,858 were injured.
Diet enacted the National Property Law 28 June governing acquisition, management and disposal of all public property.
House of Councillors resolved 18 June that the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education is invalid.
Board of Trade authorized 28 May to deal directly with foreign firms; $60,000,000 raw-cotton credit signed 6 June.
Cabinet approved a Broadcast Bill 18 June creating a Broadcasting Commission and non-profit Broadcasting Corporation of Japan.
By 20 June 673 war crimes suspects tried: 623 convicted, 95 death sentences; 1,136 interned at Sugamo.
Labor unions numbered 31,075 with 6,553,816 members; government wage standard raised to 3,791 yen.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, title pages and tables of contents for Summation No. 33 (June 1948): the four-part outline (General, Political, Economic, Social), a list of 80 charts, maps and graphs by topic with page numbers, and a topographic map of Japan listed at the end.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Condensed digest of the month's political, economic and social developments.

sections.title: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: A single sentence reports that there was no change in the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during June 1948. The page also opens Section 2 and carries its contents list.

sections.title: Political Activities
sections.summary: Part I digest of political events: the Nishio political-funds charge, a 209 to 178 nonconfidence vote, budget delays and a 30.1 billion yen revision, Ashida on Zaibatsu, the National Property Law, Democratic Party defections, the 28 June Fukui earthquake (3,195 dead), Korean school disorders, judges' pay laws and war crimes figures (Sugamo 1,136).

sections.title: Economic Activities
sections.summary: Digest of May and April economic data. Land sales reached 101,498 cho; coal output rose to 2,788,500 tons and coke hit a postwar peak; textiles, motor vehicles, power and gas were reported. Also covered are the Broadcasting Commission bill, union membership of 6.55 million, a 3,700 yen wage level, trade contracts and a 200 million dollar four-month deficit. Finance, reparations and science follow.

sections.title: Social Activities
sections.summary: Social digest: first model health center at Morioka, new Pharmaceutical, Narcotics and Marihuana laws, vital statistics and 59,196 repatriates. Education items include the 18 June resolution nullifying the Imperial Rescript on Education, boards of education and 124.9 million textbooks. Also Cardinal Spellman's visit, shrine land transfers, opinion surveys, press comment, book rights, film and music.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Government and politics, public safety, legal affairs and war crimes.

sections.title: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Nishio scandal, budget controversy, illegal transactions probes, National Property Law, local finance, Diet bills and party developments.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: The antiadministration alliance formally resolved to overthrow the Ashida cabinet, while the Nishio donation case and budget disagreements dominated politics. At month's end the government parties united to reject the opposition's nonconfidence vote against Nishio and moved gradually toward agreement on the main budget issues. The page introduces the subsections that follow.

sections.title: Nishio Controversy
sections.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Nishio's failure to report 500,000 yen in political funds threatened the cabinet and split the Social Democrats, whose left wing demanded his ouster. The 24 June nonconfidence motion lost 209 to 178, with 12 left-wingers absent or abstaining. Attorney General Suzuki said Nishio would resign after the budget passed and then be prosecuted.

sections.title: Budget Controversy
sections.summary: The budget stayed deadlocked until a 30 June compromise. Proposals included a 330 percent rail fare rise, war bond interest deferral on 78.1 billion yen and a transactions tax; Kitamura addressed the Diet 4 June. The 399 billion yen General Account was presented 8 June. Final terms set fares at 255 percent, changed 30.1 billion yen, and a 3,791 yen wage base.

sections.title: Zaibatsu Dissolution and Foreign Capital
sections.summary: Prime Minister Ashida told the Diet on 22 June that Zaibatsu dissolution was virtually complete: leaders replaced, stocks in the Holding Company Liquidation Commission's hands and purgees restricted. Economic Stabilization Board official Horigoshi said little private foreign capital could be expected soon, citing investor caution, occupation status, taxes, labor unrest and undetermined exchange rates.

sections.title: Illegal Transactions
sections.summary: Procurators uncovered hoarded military goods (Nakajima, Tohoku Metals, Fuji Sanpro) and indicted metal-company officials. The Diet committee probed Tsuji and Kamei funds, Nishio's 500,000 yen and his disbursements, Democratic Party funds via Chizaki, the Gunma coffee case (governor resigned), the Sasebo company and Finance Minister Kitamura, and Ono's perjury case.

sections.title: Government Activities
sections.summary: The National Property Law, passed 28 June, creates five classes of public property, a classification commission and Diet control over Imperial and park property. Three local finance measures seek 199.4 billion yen with new local taxes, though loan sums are disputed. Also reported are 34 prefectural conferences and the planned closing of many national local offices.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Diet bills introduced 26 May-25 June are tabulated by ministry and sponsor, from Diet-member bills to Government bills on agriculture, finance, welfare and construction. The enacted list includes the political contributions bill (19 June). Both houses reaffirmed the invalidity of the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education (18-19 June); Democrat Takahashi and Social Democrat Fujieda won by-elections.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Eight Democratic Diet members announced secession on 6 June over war bond interest deferment, and Secretary General Kimura offered to resign before staying on; Harahashi became adviser. Social Democrats approved a plan to nationalize electric power; the People's Cooperative Party offered ten budget revisions; Democratic Liberals launched an anti-Ashida campaign; the Ryokufu-kai moved toward becoming a party.

sections.title: Public Safety
sections.summary: The 28 June Fukui earthquake destroyed about 70 percent of Fukui city and killed 3,195 there, with relief by police, prisons, fire officials and tugboats. A dynamite blast at the Mitsubishi-Katsuda mine killed 62. Also covered are rail accidents, hoarded goods recovered, 196,951 April offenses, police strength, a prison population of 92,607, and April fires costing ¥950 million.

sections.title: Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The Diet passed the administrative litigation law and pay increases for judges and procurators on 25 June, and the Supreme Court set expedited rules for purge-violation cases. Atrocity investigations on hand fell to 796. Sugamo held 1,136 internees; 673 suspects had been tried by 20 June, 623 convicted and 95 sentenced to death. The Tokyo tribunal stayed adjourned since 16 April.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Thirteen sections on production, trade, prices, finance and science.

sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Tenants bought 101,498 cho in May (632,632 cho cumulative); reclamation lands 567,873 cho; land use, cooperatives, insurance, livestock slaughter, fisheries, equipment and whaling.

sections.title: Agrarian Reform
sections.summary: Tenant farmers bought 101,498 cho in May, bringing cumulative sales under the agrarian reform to 632,632 cho. The Finance Ministry stopped accepting land for taxes on 31 March, paying in land bonds instead; 200,383 cho had been transferred to the Agriculture Ministry. Reclamation holdings reached 567,873 cho, and land commissions took over reclaimed-land sales. Demonstration farms of 2,767 cho were to be sold.

sections.title: Arable Land by Prefectures
sections.summary: Arable land was 12.49 percent of Japan Proper's 36,048,047 hectares at 31 August 1947, and Hokkaido only 9.40 percent. Saga had the highest share of irrigated rice land, 20.28 percent. The farm population of 36,509,458 on 4,970,023 hectares averaged 7.345 persons per hectare. Pages 46-49 are prefectural charts and maps with no text.

sections.title: Livestock, Fisheries and Whaling
sections.summary: Agricultural cooperative federations were allowed to organize, with 75,473 directors and auditors elected by 5,470 cooperatives. Crop insurance paid out for 1947 damages, and 3,674 mutual relief organizations were registered. April slaughter fell to 4,064 tons; marine output nearly doubled to 222,509 tons. Fishing received sisal, abaca, cement and petroleum allocations. Antarctic whaling was authorized 21 June; 104 whales were taken.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: May log production was 60,355,400 cubic feet, with stockpiles down to 245,988,400; forests were overcut, especially coniferous saw timber. Charcoal and gasumaki rose. Coal output in June reached 2,788,500 tons, below quota, with May deliveries at 2,756,000 tons. Crude oil output was 15,399 kiloliters, with one new Niigata gas well; 13 of 33 minerals rose in April.

sections.title: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke output reached a postwar peak of 254,819 tons in May. Rolled steel rose 5.6 percent while pig iron and steel ingots fell; aluminum, copper, zinc and ferroalloys rose. Ammonium sulfate hit a peak of 104,765 tons. Cement fell to 141,883 tons. Shipyards completed 21 steel vessels, and tugs and barges went to Russia. Rolling stock, machine tools, bearings and textile machinery are reported.

sections.title: Manufacturing
sections.summary: Food processing was hit by depleted grain stocks, with wheat flour down sharply in April, while edible oils and fish rose. Beer rose 20 percent; tobacco, pulp and glass are covered. Electrical goods, rubber, leather and agricultural implements are reported. Standard trucks reached 1,211 and small trucks a postwar peak of 243. Typewriters rose 361 percent; watches and clocks hit a postwar peak of 197,039.

sections.title: Textile Industries
sections.summary: Fukui earthquake threatens rayon rehabilitation; raw silk 10,536 bales; cotton yarn held down while fabrics rise; rayon, wool, bast fibers, rope, garments and dyeing.

sections.title: Cotton
sections.summary: Raw cotton stocks fell as May imports dropped 3,347,000 pounds; Edward T. Robertson and Son was licensed as cotton controllers. Pure yarn output held near April at 23.9 million pounds, with spinners' stocks under a month's supply. Fabric output rose as independent weavers gained 4,678,000 square yards; allocation tickets were recalled from 36 plants, and operating looms reached 105,277.

sections.title: Silk
sections.summary: Raw silk output was 10,536 bales in May, with 20/22 denier rising to 6,155 bales; 11,856 bales were tested for export. Distributor stocks fell to 11,537 bales' worth of deliveries, one reeling mill closed, and the spring cocoon crop was estimated at 77,379,000 pounds. Silk fabric reached a postwar record of 10,631,000 square yards of filament; an 8,700,000-yard weaving program was announced.

sections.title: Artificial Fibers
sections.summary: Rayon staple and filament output set postwar records, up 589,000 and 380,000 pounds over April, while spun yarn dipped slightly. Imports included 1,700 tons of rayon pulp and the first nylon waste shipped to Japan; Kurashiki began commercial polyvinyl alcohol fiber (300 pounds). Filament fabric reached 3,368,000 square yards and spun rayon fabric 4,756,000; mills consolidated spindles and looms.

sections.title: Wool
sections.summary: May wool imports totaled 3,183 bales, but little of the 9,605 bales received since 1 April reached mills because of inspection and distribution delays. Woolen and worsted yarn output edged up on continuing imports, and fabric production rose slightly despite reduced yarn supplies, with woolen fabric at 1,571,000 square yards. Operating worsted spindles fell as mills shifted to pure yarns, and looms were consolidated.

sections.title: Hard and Bast Fibers, Garments and Finishing
sections.summary: The seventh postwar abaca shipment, 6,558 bales, arrived, lifting mill receipts of hard and bast fibers 4,112,000 pounds. Flax yarn rose 10 percent, but ramie, hemp and jute fell after a strike at the largest ramie and hemp mill. Throstle-spun materials had only about 10 days' stocks. Garment output fell except workmen's gloves; fish netting dropped as spinners withheld yarn awaiting price rises; cotton printing set a postwar record.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered motor vehicles numbered 209,002 in May, 67.3 percent operable, with freight tonnage up to 13,732,047. Railways carried 565,601,143 passengers and government rail freight reached 10,419,900 metric tons. Steel-ship coastal cargo rose 11.4 percent to 1,129,958 tons; three foreign shipping agents were licensed. Power generation was 2,974,000,000 kWh, with coal shortfalls worrying the dry season; gas output was 64.2 million cubic meters.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved a Broadcast Bill on 18 June creating an independent Broadcasting Commission and a nonprofit Broadcasting Corporation. Telephones reached 1,322,017; new radiotelephone links opened with Trinidad, Barbados, Italy and Kobe. Radio licensees numbered 6,650,046, and BCJ sought a higher listening fee. Postal savings, life insurance, mailbag and equipment figures were reported, including 988,505 vacuum tubes and 433,279 ministry employees.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Right-left struggle in unions, Labor-Farmer Liaison Council, 31,075 unions with 6.55 million members, disputes, labor relations committees, wages, employment and labor education.

sections.title: Labor and Employer Organizations
sections.summary: Left-right struggle sharpened in unions. The Labor-Farmer Liaison Council (9 June) and Tokyo Council of Independent Labor Unions (12 June, 125,000 members) were founded, and the NCIU Democratization League held its first convention. Government Railway Workers' Union elections shifted left; electric power, teachers and women communications workers met. Employers backed managerial rights. SCAP did not object to ILO observers; unions numbered 31,075 with 6,553,816 members.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: June labor relations stayed calm as grievance machinery was debated. Coal unions ratified it; Tokyo-Yokohama rail locals struck for 24 hours; the CLRC set a base wage of ¥3,923 for private railways and settled the All-Japan Express dispute at ¥4,854. Aikado Printing union leaders were convicted over production control, Toho Studio cut 1,019 jobs, and April saw 79 stoppage disputes. Labor education and publications were also reported.

sections.title: Wages, Working Conditions and Employment
sections.summary: Government wage stabilization set ¥3,700 as the base for 23 June price revisions, while government workers sought ¥5,200 and private settlements ran higher, such as ¥6,300 at All-Japan Iron and Steel. April manufacturing wages rose 14 percent. Labor standards inspections numbered 9,955, with 19,019 violations. Illegal labor supply projects, coal mine employment freeze, prison labor in Hokkaido and unemployment insurance were addressed.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Boeki Cho was authorized 28 May to deal directly with foreign firms, subject to SCAP validation. A $60 million bank credit for U.S. cotton, a 31 May sterling payment agreement and a 9 June China trade agreement were concluded. Limited tourism resumed 1 July. April imports were $60.3 million against $12.0 million of exports; the four-month deficit reached $200,186,092.

sections.title: Price and Distribution
sections.summary: Full ration needs were met from rice stocks plus imported sugar substituted for five days, though consumers complained. Collections of 1947 staple crops met or exceeded quotas by 30 June. The Cabinet approved fish and vegetable control plans 1 June, and milk, vegetable and grain prices rose. Tokyo water rates doubled, consumer prices climbed, incentive goods reached rice farmers, and 12,500 ration "ghosts" were caught.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: Licenses of nine foreign banks were broadened 14 June. Bank of Japan notes stood at 230.6 billion yen on 30 June. Reconstruction Finance Bank loans rose to 70.4 billion yen, mainly to mining and power. Fifty-one control organizations were closed. Tax collections reached 147.2 billion yen (108.7 percent of estimate); interim June budgets passed 28 May; national debt totaled 365.6 billion yen.

sections.title: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property taken into custody, mainly 39.5 million yen of cinchona bark from the Netherlands East Indies, and 246 vessels were deleted from looted lists. The SCAP Custody Account balance reached 284,957,133 yen, and foreign properties were restored. SCAP raised no objection to 775 restricted-concern applications; antitrust orders went to holding companies, and 14,122 machine tools had shipped to claimants by 30 June.

sections.title: Science and Technology
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved the Science Council Bill 8 June. The Japan Invention Association publicized inventions, and learned societies met. Japan sent astronomy papers to the International Astronomical Union, and Professor Honda discovered a new comet 3 June. Osaka's research institute reported an ephedrine pilot plant; scientific publications were issued; 1,327 Japanese Standards were in effect and patent registrations totaled 123.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health and welfare; education, religion, cultural resources and media.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Communicable diseases rise to 4,399 cases and 420 deaths in May, veterinary affairs, medical supplies, narcotics laws, public assistance, vital statistics and repatriation of 59,196.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine and Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: A model health center opened at Morioka 15 June. The House of Councillors passed the Preventive Vaccination Law and Venereal Disease Prevention Law. Eleven principal communicable diseases caused 4,399 cases and 430 deaths in May, up from 3,337 and 338. Veterinary items included fowl cholera in Akita, April meat inspection with rising condemnations, and dairy inspection of 8,588 farms.

sections.title: Medical Administration and Supply
sections.summary: The Pharmaceutical Affairs Law passed 30 June, requiring accredited pharmacists and setting penalties up to three years' imprisonment. Japan had 3,451 hospitals with 310,562 beds. Nursing courses were held for public health nurses and midwives. May medical supply output was 1.94 billion yen, with record sanitary materials; distribution fell. Narcotics laws passed 28 June; 82,324 handlers were registered.

sections.title: Public Assistance, Vital Statistics and Repatriation
sections.summary: May public assistance reached 1,911,666 persons, with welfare payments of 377 million yen. A Tokyo institution for the handicapped opened, LARA shipments arrived, and the Welfare Commissioner Law passed. Mennonite service centers and Red Cross campaign plans were approved. National Health Insurance was amended. April births were 324,393 and deaths 79,756; 59,198 persons were repatriated, mostly from Soviet areas.

sections.title: Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Rescript on Education invalidated, 1948 education budget of 26.7 billion yen, boards of education, textbooks, Cardinal Spellman visit, public opinion surveys, press, radio, film, theater, music and libraries.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: The House of Councillors reaffirmed on 18 June that the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education is invalid. The Ministry of Education budget went to the Diet with a school-building allotment of 5,381,320,000 yen, and a bill for boards of education in all communities over 10,000 was submitted. Teacher-training, social-science, adult, vocational and library programs, textbook authorization (687 manuscripts announced) and standardization of 1,850 characters are covered.

sections.title: Religion and Cultural Resources
sections.summary: Cardinal Spellman and 14 Catholic officials visited Tokyo 7 June, and clearances were approved for 46 religious workers entering Japan. Tenri, Aizen-en and Seicho no Ie reported programs and membership figures. The Ministry of Finance closed applications for transfer of state precincts (72,000 shrines, 30,000 temples), and repairs restored 28 percent of Christian churches, 16 percent of temples and 10 percent of shrines. Six Western-painting exhibitions were held, and the Government ended subsidies for contemporary art shows.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Public opinion work expanded with a 19-newspaper Newspaper Public Opinion League, sampling conferences, a radio listener survey and polls on land resettlement, daylight saving and police. Information programs covered rationing, coal, labor, savings, housing, civil liberties, health, farming and women. Press sections report 821 new book editions in May, 98 licensed foreign books, the first press-code prosecution (Nikkan Sports), and Tokyo and prefectural comment on the Nishio fund affair. Radio, film, theater, music, exhibits and two new SCAP libraries (Kanazawa, Kobe) close the section.

sections.title: Map of Japan - Topography
sections.summary: Final page of the report: a topographic map of Japan, with the back cover and a printing-plant mark. It contains no narrative text, figures or developments for the month.
